result: The authors validated a live-cell single-molecule tracking (SMT) system using HaloTag fusions of H2A and NLS proteins in mES cells. They demonstrated that H2A-HaloTag exhibits three diffusion populations (chromatin-bound CB ~72%, intermediate ID ~14%, fast diffusion FD ~14%), while HaloTag-NLS shows primarily two populations (ID ~71%, FD ~29%) with almost undetectable CB fraction.
evaluation: Claims C33-C43 provide comprehensive validation of the SMT system through multiple lines of evidence: visual inspection of tracks (C37), quantitative diffusion measurements (C39-C40), consistency with prior FRAP studies (C42), and agreement with published single-molecule reports (C43). The experimental design is well-described (C33-C36) and the CB population assignment is justified by multiple criteria (C41-C43).

result: The authors quantified distinct chromatin-binding behaviors among the five Cbx family proteins (Cbx2/4/6/7/8) in wild-type mES cells. Cbx2, Cbx7, and Cbx8 show the highest chromatin-bound levels (~26-30%), while Cbx4 has the lowest (~10%). The Cbx proteins exhibit distinct fractional sizes for fast diffusion components and similar intermediate diffusion fractions (except Cbx2).
evaluation: Claims C44-C54 present quantitative SMT measurements with error estimates for all five Cbx proteins. The data show clear differences in chromatin-binding capacities (C49-C50) and diffusion properties (C51-C53). The measurements are internally consistent and lead to the well-supported conclusion that Cbx proteins employ distinct mechanisms for chromatin interaction (C54).

result: H3K27me3 contributes significantly to targeting Cbx7 and Cbx8 to chromatin. In Eed−/− and Ezh2−/− mES cells (which lack or have reduced H3K27me3), Cbx7 and Cbx8 show greatly reduced or undetectable chromatin-bound fractions. Rescue experiments restoring Eed or Ezh2 expression recovered both H3K27me3 levels and Cbx7/Cbx8 chromatin binding.
evaluation: Claims C3, C55-C58, C92-C102 provide strong evidence through loss-of-function (C55, C92-C98) and rescue experiments (C56, C99-C102). The immunofluorescence data confirm H3K27me3 depletion (C92-C93), SMT measurements show reduced chromatin binding (C95-C97), and genetic rescue restores both marks (C99-C102). The conclusion is further supported by consistency with published ChIP-Seq data (C58).

result: H3K27me3 plays a less important role in targeting Cbx2, Cbx4, and Cbx6 to chromatin. SMT data show that removal of H3K27me3 in Eed−/− or Ezh2−/− cells has minimal effects on chromatin binding of these proteins. The authors suggest additional H3K27me3-independent mechanisms exist for targeting these Cbx proteins.
evaluation: Claims C4, C59, C67, C98 are directly supported by SMT measurements showing similar CB fractions in wild-type and knockout cells. Supporting literature (C60-C66) provides mechanistic context for H3K27me3-independent targeting, including Cbx6's lack of Ring1b interaction (C60), Cbx4's SUMO E3 ligase activity (C63), and Cbx2's ability to bind nucleosomes directly (C66). The inference of additional mechanisms (C67) is well-justified.

result: The chromodomain (CD) of Cbx7 contributes to but is not sufficient for efficient chromatin targeting. CDCbx7 alone shows <30% chromatin binding compared to full-length Cbx7, with ~65% residence time. Mutants lacking CD (Cbx7F11A, Cbx7ΔΔCD) retain detectable chromatin binding, indicating additional targeting factors exist.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C107-C114 provide quantitative SMT data comparing full-length Cbx7 with CD-only and CD-deficient mutants. The measurements show reduced but not abolished chromatin binding in CD mutants (C111-C113), supporting the conclusion that CD is necessary but insufficient (C114). The F11A mutation is validated by citation (C110), and residence time data (C69) complement the binding fraction measurements.

result: The interaction between H3K27me3 and CDCbx7 is insufficient for stabilizing Cbx7 at chromatin. Residence time measurements show that CDCbx7 (τsb = 4.7 s) and Cbx7F11A (τsb = 5.8 s) have shorter stable chromatin-bound residence times than full-length Cbx7 (τsb = 7.3 s), with reduced stable bound fractions.
evaluation: Claims C115-C122 present quantitative residence time measurements with appropriate error estimates. The data show clear differences between full-length and CD-only/CD-mutant proteins in both residence time (C116-C119) and stable bound fraction (C120). The survival probability analysis (C121) provides visual confirmation. The conclusion (C122) is well-supported by the kinetic data.

result: Genetic disruption of PRC1 complex formation facilitates Cbx7 targeting to chromatin. In Ring1a−/−/Ring1b−/− and Bmi1−/−/Mel18−/− mES cells, Cbx7 shows ~1.4-1.5 fold increased chromatin-bound fractions and longer residence times (τsb ~10.6-10.9 s) compared to wild-type cells (τsb = 7.3 s).
evaluation: Claims C5, C80, C123-C134 provide strong evidence through genetic knockout experiments in two independent PRC1 component knockouts. The SMT measurements show consistent increases in both chromatin binding (C124-C125, C128-C129) and residence time (C131-C133). The results are internally consistent and lead to the well-supported conclusion that PRC1 complex formation negatively regulates Cbx7 chromatin binding (C130, C134).

result: The CD and AT-hook-like (ATL) motif of Cbx7 constitute a functional DNA-binding unit. EMSA experiments show that neither CDCbx7 nor ATLCbx7 alone binds DNA, but CD-ATLCbx7 exhibits clear DNA-binding activity with Kd ~1.0 μM. Mutation of basic residues in ATL abolishes DNA binding.
evaluation: Claims C6, C72-C73, C135-C144 present comprehensive biochemical evidence. The EMSA data clearly demonstrate that both CD and ATL are required for DNA binding (C137-C140), with appropriate controls (C142). The Kd measurement (C143) is quantitative, and the mutational analysis (C141) confirms the importance of ATL basic residues. The comparison with H3K27me3 binding affinity (C144) provides functional context.

result: CD-ATLCbx7 preferentially recognizes double-stranded DNA over single-stranded DNA, double-stranded RNA, and single-stranded RNA. Competitive EMSA experiments show that dsDNA-2 (0.5 μM) completely displaces dsDNA-1, while much higher concentrations of ssDNA (4.0 μM), dsRNA (10 μM), and ssRNA (40 μM) fail to completely displace dsDNA-1.
evaluation: Claims C74, C145-C150 present systematic competitive binding experiments with appropriate concentration ranges. The data clearly demonstrate preferential dsDNA binding (C146-C149), with quantitative comparisons showing >8-fold selectivity for dsDNA over ssDNA and >20-fold over dsRNA. The conclusion (C150) is well-supported by the competitive binding data.

result: Cbx7 is targeted to chromatin by co-recognition of H3K27me3 and DNA through the CD-ATL module. SMT experiments with Cbx7 mutants show that deletion or mutation of ATL reduces chromatin binding to ~50% of wild-type, while deletion of both CD and ATL reduces binding to ~30%. Residence time measurements show progressive reductions in mutants lacking DNA-binding capacity.
evaluation: Claims C7, C75-C77, C151-C164 provide comprehensive in vivo validation of the biochemical findings. The SMT data show dose-dependent effects of CD and ATL deletions on chromatin binding (C151-C158) and residence time (C159-C164). The additive effect of deleting both domains (C156-C157) supports the co-recognition model. The conclusion (C77, C164) is well-supported by converging evidence from binding fractions and kinetic measurements.

result: The authors propose a hierarchical cooperation model where Cbx7-PRC1 is recruited to chromatin through CDCbx7 recognition of H3K27me3, which triggers conformational changes that enable high-affinity DNA binding by CD-ATLCbx7. The model posits that CD-ATL DNA binding is auto-inhibited and allosterically regulated by H3K27me3 interaction.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89, C165 present a mechanistic model that integrates the experimental findings. While the model is consistent with the data showing both H3K27me3 and DNA are required for efficient chromatin binding, the proposed conformational changes (C88) and allosteric regulation (C89) are speculative. No direct evidence for conformational changes or auto-inhibition is provided. The model is a reasonable hypothesis but requires additional structural and biochemical validation.

result: The introduction provides background on PRC1 and PRC2 complexes, their roles in development and disease, and the prevailing model of H3K27me3-dependent PRC1 recruitment. The authors note discrepancies between this model and biochemical data showing weak Cbx CD affinity for H3K27me3 and genome-wide data showing incomplete overlap between H3K27me3 and PRC1 binding.
evaluation: Claims C1-C32 are primarily literature citations establishing the scientific context. The claims accurately represent published work on PcG protein function (C8-C12), PRC2 and PRC1 composition (C13-C20), recruitment mechanisms in Drosophila (C21-C23), and mammalian PRC1 recruitment complexity (C24-C32). The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

result: The discussion contextualizes the findings within examples of hierarchical cooperation in chromatin regulation, citing SWR1 recruitment (DNA binding by Swc2 followed by histone modification recognition by Bdf1) and Rpd3S recruitment (multiple engagements with H3K36me3 and DNA). The authors note that H3K27me3 allosterically activates PRC2 methyltransferase activity.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79, C81-C85, C90-C91 are literature citations providing mechanistic parallels for the proposed hierarchical cooperation model. The cited examples (SWR1, Rpd3S, PRC2 allosteric activation) are accurately represented and appropriately support the conceptual framework. These claims establish precedent for the type of mechanism proposed for Cbx7.

result: The authors justify focusing on Cbx7 based on four criteria: smaller size than Cbx8, fewer conserved domains (three vs. four), Cbx7-PRC1 being the major canonical PRC1 in mES cells, and Cbx8 expression being nearly undetectable in mES cells.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 provide rationale for experimental focus. The size and domain differences (C103-C104) can be inferred from Figure 1A and 3A. The claims about Cbx7-PRC1 predominance and low Cbx8 expression (C105-C106) are supported by appropriate citations. This justification is reasonable for prioritizing Cbx7 in detailed mechanistic studies.
